This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 9: Pressure and Diffusion.
Deep underground, heat builds up pressure that pushes hot water and steam towards the surface,
where we can use its geothermal energy for electricity.
In this unit, we'll explore pressure in solids, liquids and gases,
and how particles spread out by diffusion.
Pressure is the amount of force acting on a given area.
When you pump up a bicycle tyre,
the air inside presses on the inner surface, making the tyre firm.
We calculate pressure by dividing the force by the area.
It's measured in newtons per square metre.
The triangle helps us rearrange: force equals pressure times area.
A rock weighing 5000 newtons rests on an area of 0.5 square metres.
The pressure is 5000 divided by 0.5: 10 thousand newtons per square metre.
Now the other way:
a truck exerts 10 thousand newtons per square metre over 0.4 square metres.
The force is 10 thousand times 0.4: 4000 newtons.
The same force can give very different pressures.
When you press a pushpin,
the force from your thumb is spread over the broad head,
but it's concentrated on the tiny point.
The smaller the area, the greater the pressure,
so the pin goes in easily.
Knives and axes have a very thin cutting edge, a small area,
so they exert a high pressure and cut easily.
As they're used, the edge gets wider and blunt,
so we sharpen them to keep the area small.
Skis, snowboards and surfboards do the opposite:
their large area spreads the rider's weight,
reducing the pressure so they don't sink.
A 700 newton skier on 1.4 square metres of
skis exerts just 500 newtons per square metre.
Two identical bricks have the same weight.
One lies flat on a block of soft modelling clay;
the other stands on its end.
Predict: which brick will sink deeper into the clay?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Both bricks press down on the clay with the same force.
The brick standing on its end makes a much deeper dent.
The flat brick hardly sinks at all.
Explain what you saw.
The force is the same,
but the brick on its end pushes on a much smaller area.
Pressure equals force divided by area,
so a smaller area gives a bigger pressure,
and the clay is pushed in further.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

captions: Make three holes in a bottle, one above the other,
and fill it with water.
The water spurts furthest from the bottom hole,
because the pressure there is greatest.
In a liquid, particles are close together but can slide past each other.
Their constant collisions with each other and the container walls cause pressure.
The deeper you go, the more liquid there is above, pressing down,
so the pressure increases with depth.
For every metre you dive,
the water pressure rises by about 10 thousand newtons per square metre.
That's why your ears pop.
Scuba divers who go deeper than about 40 metres must rise slowly,
stopping on the way up, to avoid decompression sickness.
Submarines are built from strong materials to withstand the huge pressure.
A diver's gauge measures the extra pressure from the
water above her at different depths in the sea.
At the surface the water adds no pressure.
At 10 metres it adds 100 kilonewtons per square metre.
The points make a straight line through zero:
every 10 metres deeper adds the same amount again.
Pause and decide: what is the water pressure at 25 metres,
and what happens to it if the diver goes twice as deep?

captions: Gas particles are always moving fast and bumping into things.
Each collision with a surface pushes on it.
That's gas pressure. In an inflated balloon, more
particles push on the inside than the outside,
so the balloon holds its shape.
More particles mean more collisions and more pressure.
Heating a gas gives its particles more energy,
so they move faster and hit the walls more often and harder:
the pressure increases. A cold beach ball from the fridge feels soft,
but warm it up and it gets harder.
Squeezing a gas into a smaller volume means the particles hit the walls more often,
so the pressure rises.
That's what happens when you sit on an exercise ball.
Air is always pressing on us.
This is atmospheric pressure.
Climb a high mountain, and the pressure falls.
Near Earth's surface, gravity pulls air particles closer together,
so the air is denser, with more collisions.
And at sea level there's more air above, pressing down.
Pressure differences let us breathe.
When your chest expands,
the pressure in your lungs drops below the air pressure outside,
so air flows in.
Gas always moves from high pressure to low pressure.
That's what causes wind, too.
Gas pressure is at work around us all the time.
Here are four everyday examples.
Pump more air into a bicycle tyre and
there are more particles hitting the inside walls,
so the pressure rises and the tyre feels firm.
Aerosol cans warn you never to heat them.
Hotter gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder,
so the pressure could burst the can.
When you suck on a straw you lower the pressure inside it.
The higher air pressure on the drink outside pushes the liquid up the straw.
High up a mountain, the air pressure is lower,
so each breath contains less oxygen.
Climbers on the highest peaks often carry oxygen tanks.
In every example, the pressure comes from moving gas particles colliding with surfaces.
Pause and think of one more example.

captions: The particle model explains pressure.
In a solid, strong forces hold particles close together, vibrating in place.
In a liquid, weaker forces let particles slide past each other,
so liquids flow, but they're still close together and can't be squashed.
In a gas, particles are far apart and move fast in all directions,
so gases are easy to compress.
When a substance is heated, its particles gain energy,
move faster and spread further apart, so it expands.
With enough energy, they break away from each other and the substance changes state,
melting and then boiling.
Expanding and changing state can greatly increase pressure.
Natural diamonds form deep in the Earth's mantle,
where the weight of the rocks above creates enormous pressure.
Combined with high temperatures, this forces carbon atoms into diamond's special crystal structure.
Today, about 99 percent of synthetic diamonds are made
in labs using high pressure and high temperature.
Scientists have even grown diamonds at normal atmospheric pressure, at 1025 degrees Celsius,
using a liquid metal alloy.
Lab-grown diamonds have many industrial uses.
One drop of food colouring is placed gently into a beaker
of cold water and another into a beaker of hot water.
Nobody stirs them. Predict: in which beaker will the colour spread out faster?
Pause and decide.
Watch. After one minute the colour has started to spread in both beakers.
After five minutes the hot water is almost evenly coloured,
but in the cold water the colour is still mostly in the middle.
Explain what you saw.
The colour spreads by diffusion:
its particles move randomly and spread from where there
are many of them to where there are few.
In hot water the particles have more energy and move faster,
so diffusion happens more quickly.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Spray perfume in one corner of a room,
and soon you can smell it everywhere.
This is diffusion: particles of one substance spreading out through another,
from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration.
It happens on its own, because particles are always moving.
Diffusion happens in liquids and gases, where particles move freely and collide randomly.
Put a tea bag in water,
and the tea particles slowly spread out until they're evenly mixed with the water particles.
Diffusion is faster when the particles are lighter, when the temperature is higher,
and when there are bigger spaces between particles.
That's why it's much faster in gases than in liquids.
Remember, diffusion isn't the same as dissolving!

Question 1: A box weighing 600 N rests on 2 m².
What pressure does it exert?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 300 N/m².
Question 2: Why does water spurt furthest from the lowest hole in a bottle?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Pressure increases with depth.
Question 3: What happens to gas pressure in a sealed container when it is heated?
Pause the video now.
Answer: It increases – particles move faster and collide more.
Question 4: Why does diffusion happen faster in gases than in liquids?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Gas particles move faster and have bigger spaces between them.
